For such a cache, the option the evidence supports is a deeper split with no rows: on Llama at half depth, RidgeFill alone retrieves 96.1 at 8K to 32K (§6.7). A selector that ignores the question, such as the protected tokens of Flash-Next’s quality mode, is the other candidate, but quality mode’s paired difference from plain RidgeFill, −-1.02 % [−-2.87 %, +0.80 %], does not establish a gain (§5.3).

Calibration length. The longest calibration document, which every set of maps uses, is about 30K tokens (30,465 tokens on the Qwen3.5-9B and 27B tokenizers, 29,009 on Qwen3-8B’s and 28,352 on Llama’s), so no map was fitted on a position much beyond that. The median calibration document is 11.2K to 11.6K tokens, depending on the tokenizer (Appendix G). The test documents run to 128K. On Llama at the primary split, RidgeFill’s filled-region retrieval falls from 79.8 at 8K to 30.3 at 64K. We have not tested whether longer calibration documents would close that gap.

The 27B. No identity-fill arm was run on this model, so its results compare RidgeFill with stock only. Of the RULER tasks, common-word extraction drops the most, by 10.0 points at 16K and 13.5 at 32K on 20 items each, with intervals that include zero; no other task moves by more than 5 points (§4.5). RULER and the agreement study stop at 32K. Above that, the only quality evidence is LongBench v2’s long group of 108 items, where RidgeFill is 0.9 points below stock with an interval from −-7.4 to +6.5 (§4.6), too wide to rule out a loss of several points. At 32K, on the 20 documents where the two arms disagree most, ten in each direction, and five near the median, the full-precision BF16 model is closer to stock than to RidgeFill on 22 of the 25 (§4.7). RidgeFill’s much lower loss on copy-heavy documents is therefore a departure from the model, not a gain. The probe’s row count, inherited from the base rules, and its 256-row window were set on development data and not swept. The value rescale was not measured on its own in the final runs. The 27B’s calibration text shares license headers, and nothing else, with 12 of LongBench v2’s Code Repository items: runs of 78 to 85 words with documents its maps were fitted on, and up to 162 words with documents only its token-frequency table counts (Appendix G).

Flash-Next. The perplexity interval runs from −-0.02 % to +4.93 % (§5.3). It does not separate the 2.65 % rise from zero, and it allows a rise of nearly 5 %. The plain RidgeFill server start did not check that switching the fill off reproduces exact. The quality-mode start did, bitwise on 6 of 6 documents, and both starts used the same container image, replaced file and arguments (§5.2). About two thirds of the routed experts are held in host memory and read over PCIe during prefill, so this deployment cannot separate the compute the fill saves from the PCIe traffic it saves (§5.3). The fork’s image is public, but its patches are not (Appendix F).

Speed, memory and compute. Every prefix row still gets a cache entry, so the fill saves no cache memory, and the maps add VRAM. On the 27B they add 1.6 to 2.9 GiB when held in GPU memory and 0.3 to 1.7 GiB when streamed from host memory (§4.4). Methods that drop tokens do save that memory. TokenGate, for example, reports 1.4 to 11.3×\times faster time to first token and 1.5 to 3.4×\times lower peak memory on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-2B (§7). Our speedups are 1.19 to 1.31×\times on the 27B, across resident and streamed maps, and 1.50 to 1.60×\times on Flash-Next. We do not compare with any token-dropping method at a matched budget. On both serving models the measured speedup is below what the skipped compute allows, and we have not profiled why (§4.4, §5.3). In the reference study, RidgeFill at 5/8 depth costs more multiply-accumulates than POP below about 46K tokens on Llama and 59K on Qwen3-8B, because of its tail and maps, so it costs more across the whole 8K to 32K needle range (§2.5, §6.4).

Follow-up analyses. The 5/8-depth comparisons with POP (§6.4) were chosen after the primary-split results were in and registered only before their own runs, so they are follow-ups. The 30 fresh documents (§6.7) were registered to test their loss results on new text, and they confirmed them; the retrieval results have no such test. The half-depth retrieval check of §6.7 was registered before it ran but stated no prediction.

Scope. The evidence comes from three reference models of 8 to 9B parameters and two serving models. Both serving models are hybrids of Gated DeltaNet and attention, both run quantized weights, and they are the only models whose speed was measured; the reference study reports multiply-accumulate counts only. Qwen3-8B runs to 32K tokens only, since it needs YaRN beyond that. Decode agreement on the reference models uses 20 documents, and LongBench v1 runs on Llama only. Flash-Next’s 64K RULER is one task, niah_single_1, on 25 samples, and its time-to-first-token medians come from prefixes of one document. The ceiling r of §2.5 assumes every layer costs the same, which neither hybrid meets, so for speed the measured numbers are the ones to use.

9 Reproducibility and recipe

Code, maps and data. The llama.cpp fork is public at https://github.com/Approximate-Science/llama.cpp-ridgefill, and the 27B runs used commit b0439f7bb on its main branch. The maps are on Hugging Face under the organization TheCacheIsALie: RidgeFill-Projector-Qwen3.8-27B-i8 (revision 69e3ea99), RidgeFill-Projector-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-i8 (revision adb763a7), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-RidgeFill-Projector (revision d2ea5faa), RidgeFill-Projector-Qwen3-8B (revision 10b9fef7) and RidgeFill-Projector-Qwen3.5-9B (revision 03363301). The technical note that preceded this paper (Johnston and Smith, 2026) reports Flash-Next numbers measured in a different engine under a different protocol; this paper’s measurements supersede them.

Everything else is in one data repository, https://github.com/Approximate-Science/ridgefill-data (tag v1.8, commit f3b343fe), kept separate from the map repositories and the engine forks. It holds the reference implementation and fit scripts, the Flash-Next run kit, the determinism fix as a diff with the hashes of both files, the per-sample RULER and per-document loss results for every arm of every deployment, the 27B and Flash-Next run records, the scripts that recompute every interval in this paper, the run ledger’s chain index and the entries the results rest on (see Registration below), and the Lean project. The three reference-model repositories hold the maps at all four splits of §6.1 as safetensors, and the data repository lists every map file by its sha256. In the data repository, code is released under Apache-2.0 and results under CC BY 4.0. The calibration and evaluation texts come from sources with different licenses, so we release their hashes, not the texts.

Pairing and determinism. In the reference study, each arm is paired with the exact run of the same session; the rows arms’ per-document differences come from a second loss run, paired with that run’s own exact. On the 27B, the fork with the fill switched off is byte-identical to upstream (§4.3). On Flash-Next, exact’s two perplexity passes agree bitwise on all 90 documents, and with the fill switched off the quality-mode start reproduces exact bitwise on 6 of 6 documents (§5.2). Both Flash-Next checks ran with the determinism fix in place.

Registration. The reference-study and Flash-Next runs were declared in the project’s run ledger, a hash-chained log, before they ran. Each entry records the claim, the predictions with their decision rules, and the hashes of the run’s configuration files. Each entry also carries the hash of the entry before it, so no entry can be edited or reordered without breaking the chain. No external registry holds the ledger. The data repository publishes its chain index, which holds the hash of every entry, and the full text of 27 of the 42 entries the results rest on. The other 15 are published as hashes only. The 27B runs of §4 are not in the published ledger: their development runs were logged on a separate branch of it, and the final runs on the A100 have no entry. Their builds, model, maps and inputs are fixed by the hashes in Appendix F and the data repository. The fresh-document confirmation (§6.7) was registered after the set was frozen and before any run on it. The half-depth retrieval check was registered before any result existed but stated no prediction. The 5/8-depth comparisons with POP were registered before their own runs but chosen after the primary-split results, so we treat them as follow-ups (§8).

Applying RidgeFill to a new model. These settings come from five models, and a new architecture or workload may need others.

  1. 1.

    Fit the maps. Run the unmodified model over calibration text, record the hidden state at the split and the input to every later layer, and solve one ridge regression per layer (§2.2), with the ridge penalty’s setting λ\lambda chosen on held-out documents (Appendix G). One capture pass serves only the splits chosen before it runs: a new split needs a new pass, and a new λ\lambda needs only new solves.

  2. 2.

    Choose the split by whether the model normalizes its queries and keys (QK-norm). On the two reference models with QK-norm, novel-token loss stays within 0.05 nats of exact at 3/8 depth. Llama-3.1-8B, which has no QK-norm, needs half depth or deeper (§6.1). Attention-selected exact rows also remove Llama’s shallow-split failure, but they lowered retrieval on Qwen3-8B (§6.5) and depend on the question (§8). For comparison, the 27B runs at 1/4 depth with 28 to 31 % of the prefix exact, and Flash-Next at half depth with no exact prefix rows.

  3. 3.

    Use an exact tail of 2,048 to 4,096 tokens, the range of the final runs. Shorter tails were tried only in exploratory work. The tail runs every layer, but it reads the filled prefix cache, so its outputs can still differ from exact.

  4. 4.

    Check that the engine with the fill switched off reproduces exact bitwise, so that every difference you measure is the fill’s.

  5. 5.

    Before shipping, measure two numbers against exact: filled-region needle retrieval and key-token Δ\DeltaNLL (§3.1). Novel-token loss alone can hide the difference: on Qwen3-8B the fitted and identity fills differ by 0.019 nats on it and by 49.6 points on retrieval (§3). A needle score near 100 can hide key-token loss (§8). If you add exact rows, compare them with the same number of random rows, and with the question hidden if the cache will serve more than one question.

Appendix F gives the builds and file hashes, Appendix G the calibration text and its overlap with the test sets, and Appendix H the exact-rows cost model, the lexical-net rules, the derivation of the ρ\rho scale and the formal statements.

Appendix A All arms at the primary split

Every arm uses the primary split and a 4,096-token tail, except POP native (its own split, one-token tail). RULER filled is filled-region accuracy (%); Δ\DeltaNLL is against exact in nats per token; decode agreement and KL are against exact’s greedy continuation (§3.1); Turn 2 is the second question of Appendix D. The controls, POP native and no fill ran RULER only at 8K to 32K, so each table gives that column for every arm and the 8K to 64K column where it exists. The per-document Δ\DeltaNLL table (342 model–document pairs on the evaluation documents and 30 on Llama-3.1-8B’s fresh documents, with every arm and depth that ran) is derived/per-document-nll.csv in the data repository. Its key is model, set and document, because 25 of the fresh documents reuse evaluation-document names.

Appendix B Additional contrasts

Paired contrasts not shown in §6, at the primary split unless the row says otherwise. RULER is filled-region accuracy in points; Δ\DeltaNLL is in nats per token.

Appendix C RULER by task and length

Filled-region samples at the primary split and tail. niah_multiquery at 8K has no filled-region sample on any model, and the no-fill arm did not run at 64K, so where a row spans 8K to 64K its no-fill cell covers 8K to 32K only.

Appendix D Second question on a once-filled cache

The second question is asked of the cache filled, and the rows chosen, for the first. The prompts are the niah_multikey_1 samples, which carry four keyed needles. The second question asks for one of the other three keys, chosen by a per-sample seed that is the same on every model. It is appended after the first answer and runs exactly on the carried cache; rows are not chosen again. An answer counts if the first seven-digit number in the reply is right, which is stricter than RULER’s substring match. Under RULER’s scorer, two cells of Table D.1 change, both for Llama’s RidgeFill alone: it goes from 57.0 to 62.0, and from 46.9 to 53.1 with the second needle in the filled region.

The test is weaker than it looks. All four needles share one template, so the rows chosen for the first question already cover a median of 85 %, 86 % and 54 % of the second needle’s tokens when that needle is in the filled region. It tests a sibling needle that the selector already favored, not an unrelated question (§8).

Appendix E RULER prompts in the serving engines

Both engines put the question and the answer format in a single user turn, prefill no answer prefix, and run with thinking off. They word the instruction differently.

  • •

    On Qwen3.8-27B (llama.cpp), the prompt keeps RULER’s question line and appends Answer with the requested answer(s) in the form: [answer prefix] <answer(s)>.

  • •

    On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (vLLM), the prompt replaces the question line with Answer the following question: [question] and adds In your answer, respond with the following format: [answer prefix]: <number>, …, with one <number> per expected value. The run’s records confirm nothing was prefilled: the model wrote the whole answer sentence itself.

Appendix F Builds and file hashes

Reference study. The three reference models are the post-trained releases (Table F.1). Llama-3.1-8B is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-9B, which Hugging Face lists as an image-and-text model, runs on its text path only. The runs used four commits of the reference implementation (Table F.2). The data repository’s code/ folder holds the implementation, and code/run-commit-diffs/ holds each run commit as a diff against it. The per-document Δ\DeltaNLL of every reference arm and depth is one CSV, derived/per-document-nll.csv. It covers 342 model–document pairs on the evaluation documents (126 on Llama-3.1-8B and on Qwen3.5-9B, 90 on Qwen3-8B) and, besides those, Llama-3.1-8B’s 30 fresh documents.

Map format. The 27B and Flash-Next maps are int8, with one bf16 scale per 128 weights of each row and a bf16 bias. The 27B release holds 48 maps, for layers 16 to 63, 1.2 GiB in all. It is in the ridgefill-projector-qwen3.8-27b-i8/ folder of its Hugging Face repository (revision 69e3ea99), next to the converted GGUF, which is unchanged since revision 07eb31cd. The Flash-Next release holds 24 maps, for layers 24 to 47, 0.60 GiB. With the terminal-state correction for the 18 Gated DeltaNet layers above the split and the token-frequency table that the protected rows use (§2.4), it comes to 0.65 GiB across 27 files. The repository’s source/ folder also holds the bf16 fit that the int8 maps were quantized from; the Flash-Next run kit copies its final map, which no reported number reads, into the engine’s files. The reference study’s primary-split maps for Llama-3.1-8B (split 12) and Qwen3-8B (split 13) are published as GGUF files for the fork, in bf16 and in Q8_0. The reference maps at all four splits are also published in bf16 as safetensors, one file per split: in a safetensors/ folder of the Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B repositories, and at the top level of the Qwen3.5-9B repository.

Serving builds. Table F.3 lists the files the final serving runs loaded. On the 27B, the fork and its commit are in §9, the flags and hardware in §4.1, and the fork’s RIDGEFILL.md gives the full server command of the measured configuration. The 27B maps file is the int8 release converted to llama.cpp’s Q8_0 format by the fork’s convert_ridgefill_to_gguf.py, and the public file has the same hash. The Flash-Next runs used the run kit at commit d1164746, in its c5/ directory, which is code/c5/ in the data repository, with that commit as a diff in code/run-commit-diffs/. Flash-Next serves our MXFP4/FP8 quantization, with MXFP4 experts and FP8 attention, made by an activation-aware quantizer with GPTQ error feedback (Frantar et al., 2023). Its engine is vLLM 0.29.0.dev0 at upstream commit 2bdbbc80 plus our fork’s patches, shipped as a public image; the patches themselves are not public. The determinism fix replaces one file in the image. The runs load the released int8 maps, dequantized to bf16 by the kit’s c5/convert.py. The timing prompts are the first 9,216, 16,384 and 32,768 tokens of chat_32768_0, a chat document from UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023) fixed before the runs.

Appendix G Calibration

Calibration text. Every map in this paper is fitted on the same 71 documents, and the Flash-Next maps add 80 more (below). Five more documents are held out to choose λ\lambda.

Reference and 27B maps. Every position of every calibration document is a row, and no document reaches the reference implementation’s cap of 32,768 tokens. The tokenizers differ, so the counts differ by model (Table G.1). The 27B maps are fitted on the activations of the served Q4_K_XL model, dequantized to bf16 and run in the reference implementation.

For each split, the ridge penalty’s setting λ\lambda (§2.2) is chosen from nine values between 10−410^{-4} and 1 by the cache-write cosine of §2.2 on the five held-out documents. It is 0.03 at every split on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3.5-9B and the 27B, and 0.01 on Qwen3-8B except at split 18, where it is 0.003.

Flash-Next maps. The Flash-Next maps are fitted on the served MXFP4/FP8 model’s own activations, captured through our vLLM fork at release 29.07.16. Both capture sessions record that release’s image, digest 2703275702ab6316ee91502df75486b421d0d661a99b04000c08859d91a42585, as the running image (data repository, provenance/fits/flashnext/capture-sessions/). The corpus is 151 documents: the 71 above, plus 80 more, the longest about 20,000 tokens. Chat-formatted copies of 102 of them are added. Each document runs whole, as one prompt, and every eighth token position becomes a row, with its full preceding context. The capture code writes only prefill steps of at least 256 tokens, so a document’s short final step is skipped. This gives 425,789 rows. The fit weights the chat rows so that they carry half the total weight, as if there were 497,846 rows. As on the reference models, no row lies beyond token 30,465. λ\lambda = 0.03 was chosen from six values between 0.001 and 0.3 by the layer-input cosine of §2.2, over ten captures: the five held-out documents and their chat copies. The terminal-state correction is fitted on 13 further prompts (§2.3). The capture and fit took about 2 hours on two R9700s.

Overlap with the test sets. Three checks compare the calibration text with the test sets. The first works in tokens, on the text as each model tokenizes it, against the 126 evaluation documents and the 30 fresh ones. No calibration document has the same hash as any of them, and no document used to fit a map shares a run of 50 or more tokens with them; the longest shared run is 47 tokens. Shorter runs are common. At eight tokens most documents share some phrase, and every shared run of 32 tokens or more is license or template boilerplate or a number sequence. One document used only to choose λ\lambda, and never fitted on, shares an 80-token license header with one fresh source-code document, and shorter pieces of it with two others. In words, that header is a 40-word run, under the 50-word rule of §6.7.

The second check works in words, against the reference study’s evaluation set and the raw pool of LongBench v1 documents. The evaluation set shares no run of 50 words with the calibration text. Of the 99 documents first assembled for calibration, 28 shared such a run with the raw pool, though never with an evaluated item, and so did one prompt for the terminal-state correction. All 28 are excluded from every map fit. Two uses remain. Flash-Next’s terminal-state correction includes that one prompt, and the token-frequency table counts the 28 documents; both Flash-Next’s protected rows and the 27B’s base-rule count use that table (§2.4). Neither check covered LongBench v2.

The third check covers it. It uses the second check’s 50-word rule and also compares whole-text hashes. It compares all 304 calibration texts with LongBench v2’s 503 items and with every 27B evaluation prompt. The 304 are every fit, λ\lambda, chat-copy and terminal-state document, plus the 28 excluded ones. No calibration text has the same hash as any evaluation text or file. Thirty-eight document–item pairs share a run of 50 or more words, and one of them is content: a novel chapter, in a different edition, that a document used only for the Flash-Next maps shares with one Single-Document QA item, over a run of 70 words. Flash-Next is not scored on LongBench v2, and the 27B’s maps never saw that document. The other pairs are license headers in Code Repository items. Four fit documents, all among those the 27B’s maps were fitted on, share runs of 78 to 85 words with five items. Six excluded documents, which only the token-frequency table counts, share up to 162 words with eleven items, four of them among those five, so 12 items in all; the longest run is a complete MIT license. No λ\lambda document or terminal-state prompt shares a 50-word run with any evaluation text, and no 27B RULER or timing prompt shares one with any calibration text. The script and its result are in the data repository.

Appendix H Derivations and formal statements

Exact rows and the cost model. An exact prefix row does the same compute in the late layers as a tail row, but it takes κ\kappa times as long there, because it shares each read of the layer weights with far fewer rows. On the 27B, the exact rows are scattered through the prompt, so the second sweep runs them in smaller, less efficient batches than the contiguous tail, and each of those micro-batches reads the late layers’ weights in full (§4.4).

On Flash-Next the sharing happens inside each expert. Flash-Next prefills in chunks of 2,048 tokens, and each late layer sends every token to 10 of its 512 routed experts. A tail chunk touches nearly every expert, so each expert’s weights are read once for about 40 tokens. In a prefix chunk under quality mode, only the protected rows run the expert blocks. On the Flash-Next run they were 3 to 10 % of each prompt’s prefix, so about 60 to 200 rows of a chunk if they spread evenly. If routing spreads evenly, those rows still touch about 70 to 98 % of the experts, so nearly the same weights are read for a tenth of the rows or fewer, about 10 to 24 times a tail row’s expert traffic per row. The routed experts held in host memory, about two thirds of them (16,042 of 24,576 per GPU), are read over PCIe; the rest, the shared expert and the attention weights stay in VRAM. The even-routing assumption is ours, and neither deployment was profiled, so both accounts are explanations that a profile would have to confirm.

So the prefill time grows in a straight line with the number EE of exact prefix rows:

τ⁡(E)=τ0+E​σ,\tau(E)=\tau_{0}+E\,\sigma,

where τ0\tau_{0} is the time with no exact rows and σ\sigma, the time one exact row adds, is κ\kappa times a tail row’s time in the late layers. If prefill time follows this model, two measured times fix the line: τ0\tau_{0}, and τ⁡(E1)\tau(E_{1}) for some number E1E_{1} of exact rows, which give σ=(τ⁡(E1)−τ0)/E1\sigma=(\tau(E_{1})-\tau_{0})/E_{1}. RidgeFill with EE exact rows is then no slower than exact prefill, whose time is τexact\tau_{\text{exact}}, when

E≤(τexact−τ0)/σ.E\leq(\tau_{\text{exact}}-\tau_{0})/\sigma.

In words, the time RidgeFill saves with no exact rows, divided by the time each exact row costs, is the number of exact rows it can afford. κ\kappa has to be measured, and the final runs did not measure it: the 27B timings cover only stock and the full configuration, and no count of exact rows was recorded for the Flash-Next timing prompts. Quality mode adds exact rows and is slower than plain RidgeFill on Flash-Next (§5.3). It also adds the terminal-state correction, but that is one addition per layer, so the rows are the likely cost; the final runs do not separate the two.

Lexical-net normalization. Words are runs of Unicode letters and number characters; punctuation, underscores and combining marks separate them. ASCII letters are lower-cased, and every other character is kept as it is. A final s is dropped from words of four or more characters unless the word ends in ss. A sentence ends at a line break; at a period, exclamation mark or question mark followed by whitespace or the end of the text; at the CJK full stop, exclamation mark or question mark; and at control, user-defined, unknown and unused tokens.

Why the terminal-state correction is scaled by ρ\rho. A Gated DeltaNet layer keeps a running state. At each token it multiplies the state by a gate between 0 and 1, which fades older tokens, and adds the token’s own update. The terminal-state correction adds a fixed offset Δ​Mℓ\Delta M_{\ell} to the state of layer ℓ\ell at the end of the prefix, scaled by ρℓ\rho_{\ell}, the filled rows’ share of that state. Under a simple model of the layer, that scale removes the fill’s shift exactly.

Take one layer. The delta rule also erases part of the old state before each write, in the direction of the token’s key; for simplicity, drop that erase term. The state after token tt is then Mt=gt​Mt−1+utM_{t}=g_{t}M_{t-1}+u_{t}. The state MtM_{t} and the update utu_{t} are matrices of the same size, one per head, and the gate gtg_{t} is one number between 0 and 1 per head and token. Unrolling over the nn prefix rows gives the state at the end of the prefix:

Mn=∑j=1nwj​uj,wj=∏k=j+1ngk.M_{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}u_{j},\qquad w_{j}=\prod_{k=j+1}^{n}g_{k}.

Row jj’s weight wjw_{j} is the product of every gate after it, and the last prefix row’s weight is 1.

The fill changes the updates of filled rows. Suppose, as an idealization, that it shifts each one by the same amount δ\delta, a matrix the size of the state. The state at the end of the prefix is then off by δ​∑j​filledwj\delta\sum_{j\,\text{filled}}w_{j}. A fully filled prefix would be off by δ​∑jwj\delta\sum_{j}w_{j}, and that is what Δ​Mℓ\Delta M_{\ell} estimates. Multiplying Δ​Mℓ\Delta M_{\ell} by

ρℓ=∑j​filledwj∑jwj,\rho_{\ell}=\frac{\sum_{j\,\text{filled}}w_{j}}{\sum_{j}w_{j}},

the filled rows’ share of the weight at the end of the prefix, gives δ​∑j​filledwj\delta\sum_{j\,\text{filled}}w_{j}, which removes the shift exactly. Any other scale leaves part of it, and the unscaled correction overshoots by the exact prefix rows’ share. Because the correction is added at the end of the prefix, the tail’s gates fade it exactly as they fade the error, so it cancels in the final state too.

Behind the exact tail, the filled rows’ share of the final state is small on layers that fade quickly (Figure 4). Suppose every gate is at most γ\gamma < 1 and the last mm rows of the prompt are exact. Each filled row then has at least mm gates after it, so the filled rows’ total weight in the final state is at most γm+γm+1+⋯=γm/(1−γ)\gamma^{m}+\gamma^{m+1}+\dots=\gamma^{m}/(1-\gamma). The total weight of all rows is at least 1, the last row’s weight, so the filled rows’ share is at most γm/(1−γ)\gamma^{m}/(1-\gamma). For γ\gamma = 0.4 and m = 16 this is 7.2×10−77.2\times 10^{-7}. Only layers whose gates stay near 1 need the correction.

The bound also holds with the erase term: two runs that receive the same last mm inputs end with states that differ by at most γm\gamma^{m} times their difference before those inputs. StCorrection.lean and GdnContraction.lean state both results (below).

Formal statements. The statements in Table H.1 are proved in Lean 4.34.1 (de Moura and Ullrich, 2021) against Mathlib v4.34.1 (The mathlib Community, 2020), in the KvaLean project (code/lean/kva_lean in the data repository). The project has 219 theorems, none left unproved (no sorry), and a full lake build passes. Every module except a shared vector-norm helper, VecNorm.lean, ends with #print axioms, which lists the axioms its proofs depend on, and each lists only the standard three: propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. All of the statements concern idealized models. They predict the sign and pattern of the splice and control results, not their size. The project also holds SoftmaxShift.lean, which the paper does not use.

Appendix I Development measurements

These measurements come from the method’s development, before the evaluation design of §3 was fixed. They support statements in §1, §2.4 and §3. They are not evidence for §4 to §6, and their sets are small. The data repository holds each one’s records under results/development/, marked with the status DEVELOPMENT, and recompute/dev_history.py recomputes every number below. Intervals are 95 % percentile bootstraps over the units named.

I.1 and the first two paragraphs of I.2 used an earlier development checkpoint: a community-modified build of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, quantized to 4 bits (IQ4_XS) and served in our own development engine. It is not the checkpoint of §5; the data repository names it. The rest used the models of §4 and §6.

I.1 Corrections from approximation theory

Each correction was fitted on 6 held-out documents and scored on 23 development prompts at split 16 with a 2,048-token tail. The measure is the relative error of the attention output, averaged over the late attention layers, against the plain fill (Table I.1). Σ\Sigma is the covariance of the fill’s error in a key.

The key-mean shift, the largest gain, was then run end to end on the same 23 prompts, with the terminal-state correction in both arms. It changed the loss on novel tokens by +0.0010 nats [−-0.0048, +0.0063]. The key temperature was not run end to end, because it added nothing on top of the shift.

Nyquist’s argument needs an error that changes slowly from one row to the next. The fill’s error does not. On three held-out documents, the correlation between a row’s error and the previous row’s, averaged over layers, is 0.17 to 0.21, and eight rows apart it is at most 0.06. Exact rows spread through the prompt in chunks did worse than the same number of exact rows at the end of the prompt in all 9 settings tried: 10, 25 and 50 % of the prompt, in chunks of 128, 256 and 512 rows. At 25 % in chunks of 256, the attention-output error was 0.26 against 0.22.

I.2 Needles in the filled region

On the development checkpoint at split 16, 60 needle prompts hid a seven-digit number at 8K, 16K and 32K tokens and five depths. With the terminal-state correction and a 2,048-token tail, 52 needles fell in the filled region; with a 4,096-token tail, 36 did. The fill retrieved 33 of 52 and 25 of 36, and every needle in the exact tail (8 of 8, 24 of 24). Of the 17 wrong numbers, 13 differ from the needle only in the last digit, for example 4729999 for 4729995. The exact model returned no wrong number, but 16 of its 60 answers held no number at all, because its reasoning used up the answer budget, so this run gives counts and no accuracy against exact.

With a corrected answer format, the exact model retrieved 60 of 60 and the fill 26 of the 36 needles in its filled region (4,096-token tail). Computing exactly the attention keys and values of the rows that hold digit tokens, 2.2 to 6.2 % of the prompt, retrieved 36 of 36. Lengthening the exact tail instead, by at least as many rows (rounded up to whole blocks of 1,568, three to ten times as many), retrieved 28 of 36.

The reference models repeat the pattern and show where it stops (Table I.2). The settings are split 12 with a 1,024-token tail and split 16 with 1,024 and 4,096 tokens; the unit is a prompt in one setting whose needle lies in the filled region. Exact digit rows help on numeric multi-key needles and do little or nothing on needles that are not numbers: five kinds of text on Llama-3.1-8B, names and phrases on Qwen3.5-9B. The fill fails on those too; at split 12, Llama-3.1-8B’s fill retrieved 0 of 44 hexadecimal identifiers, against 44 of 44 for exact. Exact rows chosen by attention, the 5 % of prefix rows that receive the most attention from the prompt’s last tokens, help on both kinds.

I.3 Fill error by token class

On Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3.5-9B at split 12, over 23 development prompts, we measured each token’s relative error in what the late layers read: the attention keys and values and, on Qwen3.5-9B, the Gated DeltaNet inputs. Across nine token classes (word starts, word pieces, numbers, punctuation, spaces and others; the 23 special tokens left out), the largest class mean is 1.08 and 1.13 times the smallest. What the error costs is concentrated. We estimated each row’s cost to first order, as the change in loss if its late attention keys and values were exact, from the gradient at the filled cache. Each document’s top 5 % of tokens hold 80 % and 63 % of that estimate’s total. Its total overstates the measured gain from making every late attention key and value exact by 2.6 and 2.4 times, so we use it to rank rows only. The token-class shares of §2.4 use the same estimate on a separate development corpus of 300 documents, cut into 801 windows on each model. There we summed the estimate’s absolute value by token class, leaving out each window’s first token, and divided each class’s share of that sum by its share of the tokens.

I.4 Checking a filled cache during decoding

On Qwen3.8-27B in a development build of the engine, a decode-time check bounds the attention each filled row receives from the current query and flags rows that cross a threshold for exact recomputation. Scoring every filled row at every step is sound and left the generated tokens unchanged; in two runs it added 7.9 to 9.7 % to decoding time at 16K and 16.9 to 18.2 % at 32K. Checking each row only every 4, 8 or 16 steps, with a watch list, costs less, but in 14 configurations at least one row that needed repair went unrepaired in 15 to 98 % of decoding steps.

I.5 Needle suites and RULER

On Qwen3.8-27B in a development build of the engine, an earlier configuration (40 % exact rows chosen by the probe, special rows exact and the value rescale) passed both of our needle suites, 96 of 96 needles, as stock did. On RULER at 16K it retrieved 8 of 20 on niah_multikey_2 and 6 of 20 on niah_multikey_3, against 20 of 20 for stock on each. After this run we stopped using our needle suites for any decision.
